findings.title: Bluetooth Device Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile every discovered radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Bluetooth interfaces that are not required.
findings.description: A Bluetooth (BR/EDR or BLE) device was detected during zero-knowledge scanning, along with its advertising data (address, address type, RSSI, name, service UUIDs, manufacturer data).
findings.impact: Confirms a live wireless attack surface and provides the address and advertised metadata needed to target every subsequent enumeration, pairing, and exploitation test.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile every discovered radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Bluetooth interfaces that are not required.

findings.title: BLE GATT Service Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Where the GATT layout itself is sensitive, require an encrypted, bonded link before service discovery is permitted.
findings.description: The GATT server of a BLE device was enumerated without prior knowledge, revealing its services, characteristics, handles and properties (read/write/notify).
findings.impact: Discloses device function and defines the read/write/subscribe attack surface; unauthenticated enumeration is the first step toward characteristic abuse.
findings._x_remediation: Where the GATT layout itself is sensitive, require an encrypted, bonded link before service discovery is permitted.

findings.title: Classic Bluetooth SDP Service Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Disable unused BR/EDR profiles; restrict SDP exposure and require authentication for sensitive services.
findings.description: Classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR) SDP service records were enumerated (RFCOMM/L2CAP channels, profiles such as SPP/DUN/PAN).
findings.impact: Exposed SDP records widen the BR/EDR attack surface and can reveal legacy profiles (PAN/BNEP, DUN) with their own vulnerability history.
findings._x_remediation: Disable unused BR/EDR profiles; restrict SDP exposure and require authentication for sensitive services.

findings.title: Static or Public Bluetooth Address — Device Trackable
findings.remediation_brief: Enable LE Privacy with frequently-rotating Resolvable Private Addresses; distribute the IRK only to bonded peers.
findings.description: The device advertises with a Public or Static-Random Bluetooth address that does not rotate, rather than a rotating Resolvable Private Address (RPA).
findings.impact: A stable address lets any passive listener track and correlate a body-worn or clinical device (and by extension a patient) across time and location, and leaks the OUI/vendor.
findings._x_remediation: Enable LE Privacy with frequently-rotating Resolvable Private Addresses; distribute the IRK only to bonded peers.

findings.title: Sensitive Identifier Broadcast in Advertising Data
findings.remediation_brief: Remove serials and patient identifiers from the advertised device name and manufacturer data; expose per-unit IDs only via an authenticated, bonded GATT read; consider BT 5.4 Encrypted Advertising Data.
findings.description: The device broadcasts a serial number, patient identifier, or other per-unit token in its advertising name or manufacturer-specific data, in the clear.
findings.impact: A stable unique identifier in advertising defeats address privacy (the string becomes the tracking key) and discloses asset/patient information to any passive listener in range.
findings._x_remediation: Remove serials and patient identifiers from the advertised device name and manufacturer data; expose per-unit IDs only via an authenticated, bonded GATT read; consider BT 5.4 Encrypted Advertising Data.

findings.title: Just Works Pairing — No MITM Protection
findings.remediation_brief: Provision real IO capability and set the MITM bit (LESC Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry); where no IO exists, use OOB pairing or an app-layer authenticated channel.
findings.description: The device negotiated Just Works pairing (SMP MITM-protection bit = 0, or an IO capability of NoInputNoOutput on either side), which provides no man-in-the-middle protection.
findings.impact: An active attacker in radio range can interpose during pairing and relay or modify the entire connection, because Just Works authenticates neither party.
findings._x_remediation: Provision real IO capability and set the MITM bit (LESC Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry); where no IO exists, use OOB pairing or an app-layer authenticated channel.

findings.title: LE Legacy Pairing — Passively Decryptable
findings.remediation_brief: Require LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256); reject SC=0 on any hardware that supports LESC (BLE 4.2+).
findings.description: The device negotiated LE Legacy pairing (SMP Secure Connections bit = 0). Legacy derives the session key from a weak Temporary Key (Just Works TK=0; Passkey Entry TK is a ~20-bit value).
findings.impact: A passively-sniffed pairing can be decrypted offline with crackle, recovering the Long-Term Key and all past and future bonded traffic for that pair.
findings._x_remediation: Require LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256); reject SC=0 on any hardware that supports LESC (BLE 4.2+).

findings.title: Static or Reused BLE Passkey
findings.remediation_brief: Use a fresh, random, per-pairing passkey that is never hard-coded, printed, or reused across units; prefer Numeric Comparison or OOB where the UI allows.
findings.description: The device authenticates LE Secure Connections pairing with a static or reused 6-digit passkey — printed on the enclosure, embedded in firmware/manual, or identical across units — rather than a fresh random per-pairing value.
findings.impact: A hard-coded or shared passkey defeats the MITM protection of LESC Passkey Entry: anyone who can read the printed/documented value can complete an authenticated man-in-the-middle relay, reducing LESC to Just Works in practice.
findings._x_remediation: Use a fresh, random, per-pairing passkey that is never hard-coded, printed, or reused across units; prefer Numeric Comparison or OOB where the UI allows.

findings.title: Bluetooth Pairing Method Confusion
findings.remediation_brief: Pin the negotiated association model, present an unambiguous 'enter' vs 'compare' UI, and prefer OOB pairing.
findings.description: A man-in-the-middle can negotiate Numeric Comparison with one device and Passkey Entry with the other in the same ceremony; both use a 6-digit value, so the user reads the number one device shows and enters it into the other, completing a stable MITM even under LESC.
findings.impact: Defeats the highest LESC/MITM security level via the human factor (CERT VU#534195): the attacker holds a persistent interposed position while both devices report a successful pairing.
findings._x_remediation: Pin the negotiated association model, present an unambiguous 'enter' vs 'compare' UI, and prefer OOB pairing.

findings.title: Bluetooth Pairing Security Downgrade Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a security floor (SC=1, MITM for sensitive functions, 16-byte key) and abort pairing on any weaker offer; re-verify the negotiated level before exposing sensitive GATT.
findings.description: The device completed pairing after a forced downgrade offer (Secure Connections cleared, IO capability set to NoInputNoOutput, and/or a reduced key size), instead of aborting.
findings.impact: A device that silently accepts SC=0 / Just Works / a short key when it can support stronger security is exploitable via an active downgrade man-in-the-middle in range.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce a security floor (SC=1, MITM for sensitive functions, 16-byte key) and abort pairing on any weaker offer; re-verify the negotiated level before exposing sensitive GATT.

findings.title: Short Bluetooth Encryption Key Negotiated
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a 16-byte encryption key floor and abort pairing/connection on any shorter negotiated size.
findings.description: The device negotiated a maximum encryption key size below 16 bytes (BLE floor is 7). Short keys reduce brute-force cost and are the BLE analogue of the KNOB attack.
findings.impact: A negotiated key near the 7-byte floor allows an attacker to brute-force the session key and decrypt or inject traffic.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce a 16-byte encryption key floor and abort pairing/connection on any shorter negotiated size.

findings.title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: ECDH Public Key Not Validated (CVE-2018-5383)
findings.remediation_brief: Update to post-2018 firmware/OS that mandates ECDH public-key on-curve validation.
findings.description: The pairing stack does not validate the peer's ECDH public key (Y-coordinate) during Secure Simple Pairing / LE Secure Connections, allowing a fixed-coordinate invalid-curve attack.
findings.impact: An in-range MITM present during pairing can force the shared secret into a small subgroup and recover the session key (~50% per attempt, retryable), fully compromising the session.
findings._x_remediation: Update to post-2018 firmware/OS that mandates ECDH public-key on-curve validation.

findings.title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: KNOB — Encryption Key Entropy Downgrade (CVE-2019-9506)
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the host to enforce a minimum encryption key entropy (>=7 octets BR/EDR, 16 for LESC) and abort shorter negotiations.
findings.description: The BR/EDR encryption key-entropy negotiation (LMP) is not integrity-protected, letting a MITM force both devices to a 1-byte (8-bit) key.
findings.impact: The reduced-entropy key is brute-forced in real time, allowing an in-range attacker with no pairing or user interaction to decrypt and inject traffic on the link.
findings._x_remediation: Patch the host to enforce a minimum encryption key entropy (>=7 octets BR/EDR, 16 for LESC) and abort shorter negotiations.

findings.title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BLUFFS — Forward/Future Secrecy Weakness (CVE-2023-24023)
findings.remediation_brief: Reject low negotiated key lengths, adopt the SIG key-derivation fix, and operate in Secure Connections Only mode.
findings.description: Weaknesses in BR/EDR session-key derivation (Core Spec 4.2-5.4) permit unilateral, repeatable session-key derivation, breaking forward and future secrecy; combined with key-length downgrade it enables MITM and impersonation across sessions.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can force reuse of a weak session key, decrypting captured traffic and impersonating a device across multiple sessions.
findings._x_remediation: Reject low negotiated key lengths, adopt the SIG key-derivation fix, and operate in Secure Connections Only mode.

findings.title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BIAS — Impersonation (CVE-2020-10135)
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Secure Connections Only mode and require mutual authentication in both directions.
findings.description: BR/EDR authentication does not mandate mutual authentication; via role-switch and SC-to-legacy downgrade an attacker impersonates a previously-paired master or slave without possessing the link key.
findings.impact: An attacker in range who knows the victim BD_ADDR can impersonate a trusted, previously-bonded device without any key material.
findings._x_remediation: Enable Secure Connections Only mode and require mutual authentication in both directions.

findings.title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BLURtooth — Cross-Transport Key Overwrite (CVE-2020-15802)
findings.remediation_brief: Apply BT 5.1 CTKD restrictions that forbid overwriting authenticated keys or downgrading key strength.
findings.description: In dual-mode devices supporting Cross-Transport Key Derivation (spec 4.2/5.0 before 5.1), an unauthenticated attacker in range can trigger CTKD to overwrite an authenticated bonding key with an unauthenticated or lower-entropy one.
findings.impact: The paired relationship can be silently weakened without user interaction, enabling MITM on a link the user believes is securely bonded.
findings._x_remediation: Apply BT 5.1 CTKD restrictions that forbid overwriting authenticated keys or downgrading key strength.

findings.title: Bluetooth Vulnerability: BLESA — BLE Reconnection Spoofing (CVE-2020-9770)
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce mandatory authenticated and encrypted reconnection before accepting any data from a previously-bonded peer.
findings.description: BLE reconnection authentication is optional and often not enforced by the client, so a central accepts spoofed data from an impersonated peripheral without re-authentication after the first bonding.
findings.impact: An attacker spoofing the peripheral BD_ADDR can feed forged data (e.g. medical telemetry) to the consuming device on reconnect, with no user interaction.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce mandatory authenticated and encrypted reconnection before accepting any data from a previously-bonded peer.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Read
findings.remediation_brief: Set encryption/authentication-required permissions on sensitive characteristics; gate PHI behind LESC-authenticated bonding.
findings.description: One or more GATT characteristics returned data over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Read Response with a value and no 0x05/0x0F/0x08 security error).
findings.impact: Any listener in range can read the exposed data with no credential; where it is PHI, telemetry, or configuration the confidentiality impact is severe.
findings._x_remediation: Set encryption/authentication-required permissions on sensitive characteristics; gate PHI behind LESC-authenticated bonding.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Write
findings.remediation_brief: Require an authenticated, encrypted, bonded link (LESC + MITM) for all writes; add application-layer authorization (signed / challenge-response commands) to control points and OTA.
findings.description: A GATT write to a device characteristic succeeded over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Write Response with no security error).
findings.impact: Unauthenticated write access permits configuration change, actuation, factory reset, or firmware/OTA abuse with no credential — the highest-impact GATT finding, and safety-critical on a medical device.
findings._x_remediation: Require an authenticated, encrypted, bonded link (LESC + MITM) for all writes; add application-layer authorization (signed / challenge-response commands) to control points and OTA.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Notification/Indication Stream
findings.remediation_brief: Require encryption on the CCCD and its source characteristic; do not start notifications before authenticated bonding.
findings.description: On an unpaired link the device granted a large ATT MTU and started notifications/indications after a CCCD write, streaming data without authentication.
findings.impact: Sensitive telemetry or PHI is exposed to any in-range listener without pairing; a large pre-auth MTU on a sensitive stream aggravates the leak.
findings._x_remediation: Require encryption on the CCCD and its source characteristic; do not start notifications before authenticated bonding.

findings.title: SweynTooth BLE SoC Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Update the BLE controller firmware/SDK to a patched release; where the SoC is end-of-life, apply architectural mitigations (restrict pairing, disable unused profiles, physical/RF controls).
findings.description: The device's BLE System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known SweynTooth firmware vulnerabilities in the Link Layer, L2CAP, SMP or ATT (crash, deadlock, or the Telink Zero-LTK Installation security bypass).
findings.impact: Depending on the SoC and SDK version, an in-range attacker can crash or deadlock the device (DoS, may require power-cycle) or, on affected Telink parts, install an all-zero LTK for arbitrary read/write — safety-relevant per FDA/CISA advisory ICS-ALERT-20-063-01.
findings._x_remediation: Update the BLE controller firmware/SDK to a patched release; where the SoC is end-of-life, apply architectural mitigations (restrict pairing, disable unused profiles, physical/RF controls).

findings.title: BrakTooth BR/EDR SoC Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Update the Bluetooth controller firmware to a patched release; for end-of-life SoCs, disable unused profiles, restrict connectability, and apply physical/RF controls.
findings.description: The device's BR/EDR System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known BrakTooth LMP/Baseband vulnerabilities (V1-V16), ranging from crashes and deadlocks to Espressif ESP32 arbitrary code execution.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can crash, deadlock, or (on ESP32) execute code on the controller; several affected parts (e.g. TI CC2564C, Qualcomm CSR8811/8510) were 'no fix planned', leaving only architectural mitigation.
findings._x_remediation: Update the Bluetooth controller firmware to a patched release; for end-of-life SoCs, disable unused profiles, restrict connectability, and apply physical/RF controls.

findings.title: BleedingTooth Linux BlueZ Kernel Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the kernel to 5.9+ (or vendor backport); set CONFIG_BT_HS=n to remove the A2MP path; rfkill unused radios.
findings.description: The Linux host behind the Bluetooth controller runs an unpatched BlueZ kernel (< 5.9), exposing the BleedingTooth family: BadKarma (L2CAP heap type-confusion), BadChoice (info leak), BadVibes (BLE ext-advertising heap overflow).
findings.impact: BadKarma chains to zero-click kernel remote code execution over BR/EDR from radio range; BadVibes needs only that the victim is scanning, with no BD_ADDR required.
findings._x_remediation: Patch the kernel to 5.9+ (or vendor backport); set CONFIG_BT_HS=n to remove the A2MP path; rfkill unused radios.

findings.title: BlueBorne Bluetooth Stack Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Apply the 2017-09+ vendor security patches; disable Bluetooth when unused.
findings.description: The host Bluetooth stack (Linux BlueZ, Android, Windows, or old iOS) predates the 2017 BlueBorne patches, exposing SDP/BNEP/L2CAP flaws that require only that Bluetooth is powered on.
findings.impact: An attacker in range can achieve remote code execution or MITM with no pairing and no user interaction; 'non-discoverable' is not a mitigation because the address is recoverable by sniffing.
findings._x_remediation: Apply the 2017-09+ vendor security patches; disable Bluetooth when unused.

findings.title: LE Secure Connections Confirmed (Passively Uncrackable)
findings.remediation_brief: Maintain LESC; additionally verify per-pairing random passkeys, no debug keys, and rejection of downgrade offers.
findings.description: The device completed LE Secure Connections pairing (ECDH P-256), confirmed on the wire by the Pairing Public Key / DHKey Check PDUs and/or a crackle result of 'LE Secure Connections'.
findings.impact: Positive assurance that the session key never crosses the air and the pairing is not passively crackable; residual risk shifts to implementation flaws (static passkey, debug keys, downgrade acceptance).
findings._x_remediation: Maintain LESC; additionally verify per-pairing random passkeys, no debug keys, and rejection of downgrade offers.

findings.title: BlueSmack / L2CAP Echo Denial of Service
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the stack for input-length validation; rate-limit/throttle L2CAP echo and connection requests; make the radio non-connectable when unused.
findings.description: The device degraded or reset under a bounded L2CAP echo / l2ping flood (BlueSmack), indicating it does not bound or rate-limit oversized echo requests.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker who knows the BD_ADDR can hang or reboot the device, denying service — critical for a safety or clinical device.
findings._x_remediation: Patch the stack for input-length validation; rate-limit/throttle L2CAP echo and connection requests; make the radio non-connectable when unused.

findings.title: Bluetooth Connection Exhaustion / l2ping Flood
findings.remediation_brief: Rate-limit inbound connection requests, cap concurrent connections, and recover gracefully; make the radio non-connectable when idle.
findings.description: Rapid L2CAP/ACL connection opens or a sustained l2ping flood exhausted the device's connection slots, causing it to refuse or reset connections.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can deny service to legitimate centrals by consuming all available connection resources.
findings._x_remediation: Rate-limit inbound connection requests, cap concurrent connections, and recover gracefully; make the radio non-connectable when idle.

findings.title: Bluetooth Link-Layer Malformed-PDU Crash
findings.remediation_brief: Update controller firmware and host stack (PDU length/format validation, buffer bounding); disable unused profiles; rate-limit.
findings.description: The device crashed or deadlocked when sent a malformed Link-Layer / HCI PDU (the generic class covering SweynTooth/BrakTooth-style firmware defects and Android BlueFrag CVE-2020-0022).
findings.impact: A malformed advertising/connect/control PDU — often broadcast with no BD_ADDR required — crashes the target and can escalate to remote code execution on vulnerable stacks.
findings._x_remediation: Update controller firmware and host stack (PDU length/format validation, buffer bounding); disable unused profiles; rate-limit.

findings.title: Bluetooth Testing SKIPPED — No Adapter or Sniffer Available
findings.remediation_brief: Attach a BlueZ adapter for active GATT/pairing work, or flash a sniffer board via Quiver (Sniffle / nRF Sniffer / ButteRFly / Ubertooth) for passive capture, then re-run the module.
findings.description: No Bluetooth adapter or sniffer was selected/available for the instance, so Bluetooth/BLE testing was not performed.
findings.impact: The Bluetooth attack surface of the device was not assessed; the absence of findings does not indicate the interface is secure.
findings._x_remediation: Attach a BlueZ adapter for active GATT/pairing work, or flash a sniffer board via Quiver (Sniffle / nRF Sniffer / ButteRFly / Ubertooth) for passive capture, then re-run the module.

findings.title: Wi-Fi Network Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile every discovered SSID/BSSID against the authorised wireless inventory; disable or shield any access point or wireless interface that is not required for the device under test.
findings.description: An 802.11 access point was detected during zero-knowledge scanning, along with its beacon/RSN metadata (SSID, BSSID, channel, privacy/cipher/AKM suites, associated clients).
findings.impact: Confirms a live wireless attack surface and provides the BSSID, channel and encryption details needed to target every subsequent per-AP encryption, WPS, PMKID/handshake, PMF and evil-twin test.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile every discovered SSID/BSSID against the authorised wireless inventory; disable interfaces that are not required.

findings.title: Open Wi-Fi Network — No Encryption
findings.remediation_brief: Deploy WPA3-SAE (or at minimum WPA2-CCMP/Enterprise) with 802.11w PMF required; never operate a medical or clinical device on an open SSID.
findings.description: The access point provides no link-layer encryption (open authentication). All frames to and from associated devices are transmitted in cleartext.
findings.impact: Any listener in radio range can passively read all traffic and actively inject or modify frames, capturing PHI/telemetry and hijacking sessions without any credential.
findings._x_remediation: Deploy WPA3-SAE with 802.11w PMF required; never run a medical device on an open SSID.

findings.title: WEP Encryption in Use
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately replace WEP with WPA3-SAE (or WPA2-CCMP with a strong passphrase) and 802.11w PMF; WEP has no secure configuration and must be decommissioned.
findings.description: The access point uses WEP, a cryptographically broken cipher whose RC4/IV key can be recovered from captured traffic using statistical (PTW), chopchop, or fragmentation attacks.
findings.impact: An attacker can recover the WEP key in minutes from ordinary captured traffic, then decrypt all traffic and join the network — a total loss of confidentiality, integrity, and access control.
findings._x_remediation: Replace WEP with WPA3-SAE or WPA2-CCMP immediately; WEP cannot be secured.

findings.title: WPA/WPA2-PSK Handshake Capturable
findings.remediation_brief: Use a long (>15 char) random WPA passphrase or migrate to WPA3-SAE, which resists offline handshake cracking; require 802.11w PMF to raise the cost of forcing a re-handshake.
findings.description: The WPA/WPA2-PSK 4-way EAPOL handshake was captured (passively, or after a bounded deauth), providing a verifiable offline oracle for the pre-shared key.
findings.impact: The captured handshake can be attacked offline at full GPU speed with dictionaries and rules; a weak, default, or reused passphrase is recovered, granting full access to the wireless network.
findings._x_remediation: Use a long random passphrase or WPA3-SAE; require PMF.

findings.title: WPA PMKID Capturable (Clientless)
findings.remediation_brief: Use a long random WPA passphrase or migrate to WPA3-SAE (not PMKID-crackable); disable PMKID/OKC caching on the AP where the platform allows.
findings.description: An RSN PMKID was solicited and captured from the AP with a single association request and no connected client (hcxdumptool -> hcxpcapngtool, hashcat mode 22000).
findings.impact: Because the PMKID is derived from the PMK, the WPA/WPA2-PSK passphrase can be recovered offline without ever capturing a client handshake; a weak or default passphrase is trivially cracked, granting full network access.
findings._x_remediation: Use a long random passphrase or WPA3-SAE; disable PMKID caching.

findings.title: WPS Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable WPS entirely (external-registrar and PIN methods). If push-button is operationally required, ensure the PIN method is off and an AP-side lockout throttles failed registrar attempts.
findings.description: The access point advertises Wi-Fi Protected Setup. The 8-digit registrar PIN is validated in two independently-checkable halves, collapsing the effective keyspace to roughly 11,000 attempts.
findings.impact: An attacker can brute-force the WPS PIN online (hours) and recover the WPA passphrase regardless of its strength, unless the AP enforces a robust failed-attempt lockout.
findings._x_remediation: Disable WPS; if unavoidable use push-button only with lockout.

findings.title: WPS Pixie-Dust Vulnerable
findings.remediation_brief: Disable WPS entirely; the underlying nonce-generation weakness cannot be configured away. Rotate the WPA passphrase after disabling, as it must be considered compromised.
findings.description: The WPS registrar generates predictable/low-entropy E-S1/E-S2 Diffie-Hellman nonces, allowing the WPS PIN to be recovered offline from a single M1-M3 exchange (the pixie-dust attack).
findings.impact: The WPS PIN — and therefore the WPA passphrase — is recovered offline in seconds with no online guessing, granting full network access regardless of passphrase strength.
findings._x_remediation: Disable WPS and rotate the passphrase; the nonce weakness is unpatchable via config.

findings.title: Missing 802.11w Management Frame Protection
findings.remediation_brief: Set Protected Management Frames to 'required' (802.11w MFPR) on the AP and device; WPA3-SAE mandates PMF. Where clients cannot support it, at minimum enable PMF-capable and prioritise a WPA3 migration.
findings.description: The network does not require 802.11w Management Frame Protection (the MFPR bit is clear in the RSN capabilities), so deauthentication and disassociation frames are unauthenticated.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can forge management frames to evict clients on demand (availability loss) and force EAPOL re-handshakes for offline PSK cracking — a reliable DoS and handshake-harvesting primitive against a wireless-dependent device.
findings._x_remediation: Require 802.11w PMF (mandatory under WPA3-SAE).

findings.title: WPA3 Transition Mode Downgrade
findings.remediation_brief: Move to WPA3-only (SAE) mode with PMF required once all clients support it; disable the WPA2 transition fallback for sensitive networks so a downgraded handshake cannot be solicited.
findings.description: The AP advertises WPA3 in transition (mixed) mode, offering both SAE (WPA3) and PSK (WPA2) AKM suites on the same SSID.
findings.impact: A rogue AP advertising only WPA2-PSK forces a supplicant to fall back to the crackable WPA2 4-way handshake (Dragonblood transition-mode downgrade); the SAE upgrade provides no protection while WPA2 fallback is accepted.
findings._x_remediation: Move to WPA3-only SAE with PMF; disable WPA2 fallback.

findings.title: Rogue Access Point / Evil Twin Feasible
findings.remediation_brief: Require WPA3-SAE with PMF (mutual authentication), or for Enterprise validate the RADIUS server certificate and pin the CA on the client so a rogue AP cannot complete association.
findings.description: The device under test associated with a rogue access point cloning the target SSID (optionally PMF-less / WPA2-only) instead of authenticating the genuine AP.
findings.impact: Without server-certificate validation, PMF, or mutually-authenticated association, an evil twin in range captures the device onto an attacker-controlled network to intercept and modify its traffic and harvest credentials (captive-portal or EAP relay).
findings._x_remediation: Require WPA3-SAE+PMF or validate/pin the EAP server certificate.

findings.title: Wi-Fi Deauthentication Denial of Service
findings.remediation_brief: Enable 802.11w Protected Management Frames as REQUIRED (mandatory under WPA3-SAE) so forged deauth/disassoc frames are rejected; add wired or failover connectivity for safety-critical functions.
findings.description: A bounded burst of forged deauthentication/disassociation frames disconnected the device under test from its network, confirming that unauthenticated management frames are honoured (no 802.11w PMF required).
findings.impact: Any in-range attacker can persistently deny the wireless-dependent device network connectivity by spoofing management frames — a serious availability risk for a medical or clinical device that relies on wireless data or control.
findings._x_remediation: Require 802.11w PMF; provide wired/failover connectivity for critical functions.

findings.title: Wi-Fi Testing SKIPPED — No Wireless Adapter or Toolkit Available
findings.remediation_brief: Attach an Alfa AWUS036ACM/NEH/H (or drive the WiFi Pineapple Mark VII) and install the aircrack-ng suite (plus hcxdumptool/hcxtools, reaver, iw), then re-run the WiFi module to complete 802.11 coverage.
findings.description: 802.11 testing was not performed for this instance because no monitor-mode adapter was selected, a non-capture device (e.g. WiFi Duck) was selected, or the aircrack-ng suite was not installed.
findings.impact: The device's wireless attack surface was not assessed; open/WEP encryption, WPS/pixie-dust, capturable handshakes/PMKID, missing PMF, and evil-twin exposure remain unverified until the module is re-run with proper hardware and tooling.
findings._x_remediation: Attach a monitor-mode adapter and install aircrack-ng, then re-run.

findings.title: Sub-GHz Signal Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Inventory the emitter, band, and modulation; determine whether the transmission is in scope and whether it carries device data or control.
findings.description: An active sub-GHz (300-928 MHz) transmission from the device under test was detected and/or decoded during a zero-knowledge spectrum survey.
findings.impact: The presence of a sub-GHz radio link expands the device's remotely-reachable attack surface; a listener in RF range can begin characterising and targeting the channel.
findings._x_remediation: Inventory the emitter, band, and modulation; determine whether the transmission is in scope and whether it carries device data or control.

findings.title: Unencrypted Sub-GHz Telemetry Decoded
findings.remediation_brief: Encrypt the RF payload with an authenticated cipher, or carry sensitive telemetry over an authenticated encrypted channel; never transmit patient or asset data as cleartext RF.
findings.description: rtl_433 decoded the device's sub-GHz sensor/telemetry frames in the clear, recovering payload fields with no key, which proves the link carries device data with no transport encryption.
findings.impact: Any passive attacker in radio range can read, log, and correlate the device's telemetry over time, disclosing operational state and potentially sensitive (PHI/asset) data without ever touching the device.
findings._x_remediation: Encrypt the RF payload with an authenticated cipher, or carry sensitive telemetry over an authenticated encrypted channel; never transmit patient or asset data as cleartext RF.

findings.title: Fixed-Code Sub-GHz Remote — Replayable
findings.remediation_brief: Replace fixed-code remotes with a rolling-code scheme or, preferably, an authenticated challenge-response link with anti-replay counters; treat the transmitted code as a credential, not an identifier.
findings.description: A fixed-code (static OOK/ASK) sub-GHz remote or command protocol was decoded, meaning the device transmits the identical code on every actuation with no changing element.
findings.impact: A single captured frame can be re-transmitted verbatim to reproduce the command (garage/gate/relay/keyfob class); the captured static code IS the credential, so anyone who records one press controls the device.
findings._x_remediation: Replace fixed-code remotes with a rolling-code scheme or, preferably, an authenticated challenge-response link with anti-replay counters; treat the transmitted code as a credential, not an identifier.

findings.title: Rolling-Code Sub-GHz Remote Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Keep firmware current, enforce a tight rolling-counter resync window, prefer AES-based rolling schemes over legacy KeeLoq, and consider bidirectional authenticated pairing.
findings.description: A rolling-code (KeeLoq/HCS/Security+ class) sub-GHz remote was detected — a positive control that defeats naive single-frame replay.
findings.impact: Rolling codes still fall to jam-and-capture ('RollJam') and, for some legacy KeeLoq/fixed-seed variants, to key/seed-recovery attacks, so the control is not absolute and should be validated for counter-window and cipher strength.
findings._x_remediation: Keep firmware current, enforce a tight rolling-counter resync window, prefer AES-based rolling schemes over legacy KeeLoq, and consider bidirectional authenticated pairing.

findings.title: Sub-GHz Replay Attack Feasible
findings.remediation_brief: Adopt authenticated, anti-replay commanding (rolling counter plus MAC, or challenge-response); reject any frame whose counter or nonce has already been observed.
findings.description: A captured sub-GHz command was re-transmitted (operator-confirmed, benign) and the device under test acted on it, confirming a working replay attack with no rolling counter, nonce, or authentication preventing frame reuse.
findings.impact: An attacker who records one legitimate transmission can reproduce the command at will — unlocking, actuating, or otherwise controlling the device remotely without any credential.
findings._x_remediation: Adopt authenticated, anti-replay commanding (rolling counter plus MAC, or challenge-response); reject any frame whose counter or nonce has already been observed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Sub-GHz Command Channel (OOK/FSK)
findings.remediation_brief: Require signed/authenticated commands (HMAC or public-key) with a monotonic counter or nonce, and reject any unauthenticated or malformed frame at the receiver.
findings.description: The device's sub-GHz control channel accepts commands with no authentication of the sender — the demodulated OOK/FSK frame is a bare command carrying no signature or nonce.
findings.impact: Any attacker able to transmit on the band can craft and inject commands the device will act on, achieving unauthenticated remote control of the device's functions.
findings._x_remediation: Require signed/authenticated commands (HMAC or public-key) with a monotonic counter or nonce, and reject any unauthenticated or malformed frame at the receiver.

findings.title: Missing Message Authentication on Sub-GHz Link
findings.remediation_brief: Add per-message authentication (an AEAD tag or digital signature) and reject frames that fail integrity verification.
findings.description: No message-integrity or authentication field (MAC/signature) was observed on the device's sub-GHz frames, so their contents cannot be verified as genuine or unmodified.
findings.impact: Frame contents can be forged, altered, or replayed and the device cannot tell the difference, undermining the trustworthiness of every command and telemetry value on the link.
findings._x_remediation: Add per-message authentication (an AEAD tag or digital signature) and reject frames that fail integrity verification.

findings.title: Sub-GHz Jamming Susceptibility
findings.remediation_brief: Add loss-of-link / jamming detection with a defined fail-safe state, use frequency agility or a diverse secondary channel for safety-critical control, and alert on sustained RF interference.
findings.description: Under a controlled, operator-observed bench test the device's sub-GHz link was disrupted by narrowband jamming, denying legitimate commands and telemetry.
findings.impact: Low-power ISM control channels have no inherent jamming resistance, so an attacker can deny the device's RF link (and, via jam-and-capture, harvest rolling codes); if the channel is safety-critical the availability loss may have physical consequences.
findings._x_remediation: Add loss-of-link / jamming detection with a defined fail-safe state, use frequency agility or a diverse secondary channel for safety-critical control, and alert on sustained RF interference.

findings.title: Sub-GHz Testing SKIPPED — No SDR/Radio Hardware Available
findings.remediation_brief: Attach an RTL-SDR or HackRF for spectrum survey and rtl_433 decode, or a YARD Stick One / CatSniffer / Flipper Zero for capture-and-replay, then re-run the SubGHz module.
findings.description: No sub-GHz radio or host CLI toolchain was available for this instance, so 300-928 MHz RF testing was not performed and this interface was not assessed.
findings.impact: The device's sub-GHz attack surface remains unassessed; fixed-code, replay, cleartext-telemetry, and jamming weaknesses cannot be ruled out until a radio is attached and the module re-run.
findings._x_remediation: Attach an RTL-SDR or HackRF for spectrum survey and rtl_433 decode, or a YARD Stick One / CatSniffer / Flipper Zero for capture-and-replay, then re-run the SubGHz module.

findings.title: UWB Device Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile every discovered UWB anchor/tag against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield UWB interfaces that are not required.
findings.description: A UWB (IEEE 802.15.4z / 802.15.4a) device was detected during passive capture, along with the frame types observed (blink, poll/response/final ranging) and its transmitted address.
findings.impact: Confirms a live UWB ranging/RTLS attack surface (asset-tracking tag/anchor or secure-access ranging peer) and provides the address and frame context needed to target subsequent ranging-security tests.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile every discovered UWB anchor/tag against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield UWB interfaces that are not required.

findings.title: UWB Testing SKIPPED — No Sniffer or UWB Hardware Available
findings.remediation_brief: Flash a UWB sniffer via Quiver or import a DW3000/UCI capture, then re-run the UWB module to complete the assessment.
findings.description: Gearbox attempted UWB assessment but no UWB sniffer board was selected and no sniffer binary or capture file was available, so UWB testing was NOT performed.
findings.impact: No assurance can be given about the UWB ranging/RTLS interface — its secure-ranging posture is unknown until a sniffer is flashed (Heltec / DWM3001CDK / DWM3000EVB) or a DW3000/UCI capture is imported and the module is re-run.
findings._x_remediation: Flash a UWB sniffer via Quiver or import a DW3000/UCI capture, then re-run the UWB module to complete the assessment.

findings.title: UWB Ranging Without Scrambled Timestamp Sequence (STS)
findings.remediation_brief: Enable IEEE 802.15.4z HRP secure ranging with STS (FiRa OWR/PDoA or DS-TWR with STS) provisioned via a per-session key; disable legacy 802.15.4a ranging.
findings.description: The UWB ranging exchange does not carry a Scrambled Timestamp Sequence (STS mode 0 / disabled, or a legacy 802.15.4a device). STS is the IEEE 802.15.4z cryptographic PHY field that binds the ranging timestamp to a secret.
findings.impact: Without STS the time-of-flight measurement is unauthenticated and can be forged, so relay, replay and distance-reduction attacks against proximity-based access control or RTLS are not cryptographically prevented.
findings._x_remediation: Enable IEEE 802.15.4z HRP secure ranging with STS (FiRa OWR/PDoA or DS-TWR with STS) provisioned via a per-session key; disable legacy 802.15.4a ranging.

findings.title: Unauthenticated UWB Ranging Exchange
findings.remediation_brief: Require STS-authenticated secure ranging and reject ranging rounds that omit or fail STS verification; bind the ranging result to an authenticated session.
findings.description: Ranging frames are exchanged without cryptographic authentication of the timestamp, so a receiver cannot verify that a poll/response/final frame actually originated from the claimed peer at the measured distance.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated ranging is the root enabler of relay and distance-reduction attacks: any device can participate in or forge a ranging round, spoofing presence and distance for access control or asset tracking.
findings._x_remediation: Require STS-authenticated secure ranging and reject ranging rounds that omit or fail STS verification; bind the ranging result to an authenticated session.

findings.title: UWB Ranging Susceptible to Distance-Reduction (Ghost Peak) Attack
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce STS with a minimum acceptable STS quality/figure-of-merit, reject ranging with low STS confidence, and add an application-layer distance bound and multi-anchor cross-check.
findings.description: Without enforced STS integrity, an over-the-air adversary can inject an early cipher-guessed STS/preamble to make the ranging peer measure a shorter-than-actual distance (the 'Ghost Peak' attack, USENIX Security 2022, demonstrated on Apple U1, NXP SR040/SR150 and Qorvo DW3000).
findings.impact: Where UWB gates physical access or presence (secure entry, unlock-on-approach, RTLS geofencing), an attacker can appear 'in range' from outside the intended zone and defeat proximity-based security.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce STS with a minimum acceptable STS quality/figure-of-merit, reject ranging with low STS confidence, and add an application-layer distance bound and multi-anchor cross-check.

findings.title: UWB Ranging Susceptible to Relay Attack
findings.remediation_brief: Enable STS secure ranging and bind the ranging result to an authenticated session; never treat a UWB distance as trustworthy without STS verification.
findings.description: An attacker relaying UWB ranging frames between a genuine tag and anchor can make a far peer appear in proximity. STS-based secure ranging binds the timing to a secret and is the defined mitigation; its absence leaves proximity guarantees unenforced.
findings.impact: Relay of the ranging exchange spoofs proximity for access control and RTLS, letting an attacker unlock/authorise or misplace a tracked asset from outside the intended range.
findings._x_remediation: Enable STS secure ranging and bind the ranging result to an authenticated session; never treat a UWB distance as trustworthy without STS verification.

findings.title: Replay of UWB Ranging Frames Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Derive a fresh STS per ranging session from a monotonic counter/nonce and reject frames whose STS does not match the current session.
findings.description: Previously-captured UWB ranging frames (poll/response/final or blink) were replayed and accepted by the ranging peer, showing the exchange lacks a per-session freshness guarantee (fresh STS / nonce / counter).
findings.impact: Replayable ranging enables spoofed presence and distance in RTLS and access-control use — a recorded exchange can be reused to re-assert proximity at will.
findings._x_remediation: Derive a fresh STS per ranging session from a monotonic counter/nonce and reject frames whose STS does not match the current session.

findings.title: Cleartext UWB Positioning or Payload Data
findings.remediation_brief: Encrypt and authenticate the ranging-result and any MAC payload at the application layer; do not broadcast resolved positions or asset identifiers in cleartext.
findings.description: Positioning data (measured distance/coordinates) or a MAC-layer payload was observed in the clear in the UWB capture, with no application-layer encryption of the ranging result or asset identifier.
findings.impact: Cleartext RTLS position data discloses the location of tracked assets (and, in a clinical setting, potentially staff or patients) to any passive UWB listener, defeating location privacy.
findings._x_remediation: Encrypt and authenticate the ranging-result and any MAC payload at the application layer; do not broadcast resolved positions or asset identifiers in cleartext.

findings.title: UWB Static or Non-Rotating Ranging Key (STS Reuse)
findings.remediation_brief: Provision a per-session STS from a rotating key (FiRa dynamic STS / per-session key derivation); never ship a fixed STS_KEY/STS_IV in firmware.
findings.description: STS is present but appears to be derived from a static or reused seed/key rather than rotated per ranging session (observable as a repeating STS pattern), or a fixed STS_KEY/STS_IV is shipped in firmware.
findings.impact: A predictable or repeating STS erodes the integrity guarantee it is meant to provide, moving the system back toward replay and distance-manipulation exposure.
findings._x_remediation: Provision a per-session STS from a rotating key (FiRa dynamic STS / per-session key derivation); never ship a fixed STS_KEY/STS_IV in firmware.

findings.title: UWB Ranging Susceptible to Jamming / Denial of Service
findings.remediation_brief: Define a safe fail state on ranging loss, add jam/interference detection and alerting, and avoid using UWB ranging as the sole gate for safety-critical access.
findings.description: Under a co-channel UWB jammer (UWBAD-class attack with COTS chips) the DUT's ranging was denied, confirming a denial-of-service exposure of the ranging link.
findings.impact: Loss of ranging can drop safety/asset-tracking (RTLS goes blind) or push a UWB access-control system into an unsafe fail state (fail-open or fail-closed).
findings._x_remediation: Define a safe fail state on ranging loss, add jam/interference detection and alerting, and avoid using UWB ranging as the sole gate for safety-critical access.

findings.title: UWB Legacy (Pre-802.15.4z) Ranging — No Secure Ranging Support
findings.remediation_brief: Replace legacy 802.15.4a-only UWB parts with 802.15.4z STS-capable silicon (e.g. DW3000-class) for access control or safety-critical asset tracking.
findings.description: The device supports only pre-802.15.4z (802.15.4a HRP) ranging, which has no secure-ranging (STS) capability at all and cannot be made secure by configuration.
findings.impact: A legacy-only UWB part offers no cryptographic protection for ranging, so any security-relevant proximity/distance use is inherently spoofable and the part must be replaced rather than reconfigured.
findings._x_remediation: Replace legacy 802.15.4a-only UWB parts with 802.15.4z STS-capable silicon (e.g. DW3000-class) for access control or safety-critical asset tracking.

findings.title: UWB Device Trackable via Static Address in Blink Frames
findings.remediation_brief: Rotate the tag's transmitted address/identifier (privacy-preserving randomised addressing) and expose the stable identity only under an authenticated session.
findings.description: UWB blink/ranging frames broadcast a stable device address (EUI-64 or fixed 16-bit short address) in every transmission, with no privacy-preserving address rotation.
findings.impact: A tag that emits a fixed address in every blink can be tracked and correlated to the asset (or person) it is attached to by any passive UWB receiver, defeating location privacy for the RTLS deployment.
findings._x_remediation: Rotate the tag's transmitted address/identifier (privacy-preserving randomised addressing) and expose the stable identity only under an authenticated session.

findings.title: Smart Card Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile every detected card against the authorised asset inventory; disable unused card-based authentication paths.
findings.description: A smart card was detected in a PC/SC reader during zero-knowledge scanning, along with its Answer-To-Reset (ATR).
findings.impact: Confirms a live smart-card authentication surface and provides the ATR/reader context needed to target every subsequent fingerprint, APDU, and key test.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile every detected card against the authorised asset inventory; disable unused card-based authentication paths.

findings.title: Smart Card Reader Detected
findings.remediation_brief: No action required for the reader itself; ensure reader firmware is current and only authorised readers are attached to production hosts.
findings.description: A PC/SC (CCID) smart-card reader was enumerated on the test host, providing the contact/contactless channel used for card assessment.
findings.impact: Establishes the reader interface used to reach the card; benign on its own but scopes the physical attack surface.
findings._x_remediation: No action required for the reader itself; ensure reader firmware is current and only authorised readers are attached to production hosts.

findings.title: Smart Card ATR Fingerprinted
findings.remediation_brief: ATR disclosure is inherent to ISO-7816 and cannot be suppressed; compensate by ensuring the identified platform is fully patched and its default keys/PINs are rotated.
findings.description: The card's Answer-To-Reset (ATR) was captured and analysed, disclosing the card platform, chip, and card operating system.
findings.impact: The ATR reveals the exact card OS/chip, letting an attacker select platform-specific attacks (known default keys, applet exploits, CVM weaknesses) and defines the surface tested in later phases.
findings._x_remediation: ATR disclosure is inherent to ISO-7816 and cannot be suppressed; compensate by ensuring the identified platform is fully patched and its default keys/PINs are rotated.

findings.title: Predictable Smart Card Serial Number
findings.remediation_brief: Issue cards with cryptographically-random, high-entropy serial/UID values; never derive the identifier from a sequential batch counter.
findings.description: The card serial/UID returned by the card is low-entropy, sequential, or otherwise predictable rather than cryptographically random.
findings.impact: A guessable or sequential serial lets an attacker enumerate valid card identities, forge enrolment records, or correlate a card to a holder, undermining any control that trusts the serial as an identifier.
findings._x_remediation: Issue cards with cryptographically-random, high-entropy serial/UID values; never derive the identifier from a sequential batch counter.

findings.title: Weak or Absent Cardholder Verification Method
findings.remediation_brief: Define and enforce a CVM (PIN, PACE, or on-card biometric) access condition on every protected file and command; verify the card returns 0x6982 for unauthenticated access.
findings.description: The card served sensitive file content in response to raw READ BINARY APDUs with no Cardholder Verification Method enforced (no PIN required; the card did not answer 0x6982 'security status not satisfied').
findings.impact: With no CVM, mere possession of the card is sufficient to access protected data and operations — there is effectively no authentication, so a lost or briefly-borrowed card yields full access.
findings._x_remediation: Define and enforce a CVM (PIN, PACE, or on-card biometric) access condition on every protected file and command; verify the card returns 0x6982 for unauthenticated access.

findings.title: Unauthenticated APDU Access to Sensitive File
findings.remediation_brief: Protect sensitive elementary files with a CVM access condition and enforce it in the card OS access rules; require secure messaging for READ BINARY on protected files.
findings.description: An elementary file was read via a raw READ BINARY APDU that returned 0x9000 with data without any prior VERIFY/cardholder verification being presented.
findings.impact: Any party with brief physical access to the card and a low-cost reader can extract the file's contents (asset data, credentials, holder identifiers) directly, with no PIN or key.
findings._x_remediation: Protect sensitive elementary files with a CVM access condition and enforce it in the card OS access rules; require secure messaging for READ BINARY on protected files.

findings.title: Default GlobalPlatform Card Manager Keys
findings.remediation_brief: Rotate the ISD keys (ENC/MAC/KEK) to unique, per-card random values before deployment via GlobalPlatform PUT KEY; never ship cards on the 40..4F default key set.
findings.description: The card's GlobalPlatform Issuer Security Domain authenticated an SCP secure channel using the default test key set (40..4F / 404142434445464748494A4B4C4D4E4F).
findings.impact: An attacker with the card can open the same authenticated channel to install, delete, or replace applets and read/rotate keys — a full compromise of the card manager and everything the card protects.
findings._x_remediation: Rotate the ISD keys (ENC/MAC/KEK) to unique, per-card random values before deployment via GlobalPlatform PUT KEY; never ship cards on the 40..4F default key set.

findings.title: Cleartext Data Object Readable on Smart Card
findings.remediation_brief: Store sensitive data objects encrypted or behind a CVM; do not return holder/asset identifiers from unauthenticated files.
findings.description: Data read from the card without authentication contains cleartext printable strings (asset, holder, or configuration information stored and returned in the clear).
findings.impact: Sensitive data objects returned in the clear disclose asset/holder/configuration information to anyone who can read the card, aiding cloning, social engineering, or privacy compromise.
findings._x_remediation: Store sensitive data objects encrypted or behind a CVM; do not return holder/asset identifiers from unauthenticated files.

findings.title: Default or Known Smart Card PIN Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Force a PIN change away from all factory defaults at first use; enforce PIN complexity and a low retry counter with a secure unblock (PUK) procedure.
findings.description: The card accepted a well-known factory default PIN via an ISO-7816 VERIFY command (SW 0x9000) during an operator-confirmed, single-attempt test.
findings.impact: Anyone in possession of the card can satisfy cardholder verification with a published default PIN and unlock CVM-protected files and operations, defeating the PIN control entirely.
findings._x_remediation: Force a PIN change away from all factory defaults at first use; enforce PIN complexity and a low retry counter with a secure unblock (PUK) procedure.

findings.title: Insecure GlobalPlatform Card Lifecycle State
findings.remediation_brief: Transition the card to the SECURED lifecycle state (and lock the card manager) as part of issuance so pre-personalisation management commands are no longer accepted.
findings.description: The GlobalPlatform card lifecycle state is OP_READY or INITIALIZED rather than SECURED, meaning the card manager was never transitioned to its locked production state.
findings.impact: A card left in a pre-issuance lifecycle state permits card-content management and key-setup operations that should be closed off once the card is issued, widening the window for applet/key tampering.
findings._x_remediation: Transition the card to the SECURED lifecycle state (and lock the card manager) as part of issuance so pre-personalisation management commands are no longer accepted.

findings.title: No Secure Messaging — Cleartext APDU Channel
findings.remediation_brief: Mandate GlobalPlatform / ISO-7816 secure messaging (C-MAC + C-ENC) for all commands that carry or return sensitive data.
findings.description: The card returned sensitive file data over a cleartext (plain) APDU channel with no secure messaging (C-MAC/C-ENC) applied.
findings.impact: A passive USB-CCID or contactless interceptor can capture the command/response exchange verbatim, recovering sensitive data and enabling replay of the observed commands.
findings._x_remediation: Mandate GlobalPlatform / ISO-7816 secure messaging (C-MAC + C-ENC) for all commands that carry or return sensitive data.

findings.title: SmartCard Testing SKIPPED — No PC/SC Reader or Tools Available
findings.remediation_brief: Connect an Identiv SCR3310 (or any PC/SC) reader, install pcsc-tools, opensc, and GlobalPlatformPro (gp), start pcscd, and re-run the SmartCard module.
findings.description: Smart-card testing was not performed because the required PC/SC toolchain (pcsc_scan / opensc-tool) or reader was unavailable; the module honestly recorded that no card test ran.
findings.impact: No assurance can be drawn about the device's smart-card authentication posture — the interface remains untested until a reader and the PC/SC tools are present.
findings._x_remediation: Connect an Identiv SCR3310 (or any PC/SC) reader, install pcsc-tools, opensc, and GlobalPlatformPro (gp), start pcscd, and re-run the SmartCard module.

findings.title: Z-Wave Device Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile every discovered Z-Wave HomeID/NodeID against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Z-Wave interfaces that are not required.
findings.description: A Z-Wave network was detected during passive sub-GHz (868/908 MHz) capture, along with its cleartext frame header data (HomeID and one or more NodeIDs).
findings.impact: Confirms a live Z-Wave mesh within RF range and provides the HomeID/NodeID needed to target every subsequent enumeration and security test.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile every discovered Z-Wave HomeID/NodeID against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Z-Wave interfaces that are not required.

findings.title: Z-Wave Network Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Z-Wave frame headers are inherently cleartext; minimise information leakage by enforcing S2 on all traffic and physically limiting RF exposure of the mesh.
findings.description: The Z-Wave mesh was enumerated passively from cleartext frame headers, disclosing the HomeID, the set of NodeIDs, and the command-class traffic exchanged between the controller and its slaves.
findings.impact: Maps the controller/slave topology and per-node command-class usage, letting an attacker identify locks, switches, and sensors and plan targeted forge/replay attacks against specific nodes.
findings._x_remediation: Z-Wave frame headers are inherently cleartext; minimise information leakage by enforcing S2 on all traffic and physically limiting RF exposure of the mesh.

findings.title: Unencrypted Z-Wave Control Frames
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce S2 (Security_2) on every node, remove nodes that cannot be securely included, and never operate actuators or locks over unencrypted command classes.
findings.description: Actionable Z-Wave control traffic (e.g. Binary Switch, Multilevel Switch, Door Lock, Alarm) was observed in the clear, with no S0 (CC 0x98) or S2 (CC 0x9F) encapsulation.
findings.impact: Any passive listener can read device state, and any attacker with a TX-capable radio can forge or replay commands — unlocking doors, toggling actuators, or suppressing alarms — with no key required.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce S2 (Security_2) on every node, remove nodes that cannot be securely included, and never operate actuators or locks over unencrypted command classes.

findings.title: Z-Wave S0 Legacy Security Class in Use
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate all nodes to S2; retire S0-only devices. If S0 is unavoidable, perform inclusion inside a shielded enclosure so the key exchange cannot be sniffed.
findings.description: The network uses the legacy S0 Security command class (CC 0x98), which relies on AES-OFB/CBC-MAC with a network key exchanged at inclusion under a hardcoded all-zero temporary key and lacks S2's anti-replay and forward-secrecy protections.
findings.impact: An attacker who captures a device inclusion recovers the S0 network key and can decrypt and forge all S0 traffic; S0 also permits replay that S2 would reject.
findings._x_remediation: Migrate all nodes to S2; retire S0-only devices. If S0 is unavoidable, perform inclusion inside a shielded enclosure so the key exchange cannot be sniffed.

findings.title: Z-Wave S0 Network Key Extractable on Inclusion
findings.remediation_brief: Use S2 (ECDH-authenticated key exchange with out-of-band DSK) so the network key is never sent under a hardcoded key; shield any required S0 inclusion.
findings.description: Because the network uses S0, its network key is derivable by any attacker who captures a device inclusion: the Network Key Set frame is encrypted only under the well-known temporary key 0x00000000000000000000000000000000, so the S0 network key can be extracted offline.
findings.impact: Recovering the S0 network key lets an attacker decrypt every past and future S0 frame and forge authenticated commands (unlock doors, actuate devices); a node re-included after a power loss re-exposes the key.
findings._x_remediation: Use S2 (ECDH-authenticated key exchange with out-of-band DSK) so the network key is never sent under a hardcoded key; shield any required S0 inclusion.

findings.title: Z-Wave S2 Security Downgrade to S0 Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce S2-only inclusion with no S0 fallback; reject any KEX_REPORT that requests a lower security class; require out-of-band DSK verification at inclusion.
findings.description: During inclusion the controller accepted a downgrade of the negotiated security class from S2 to the legacy S0 command class (the 'Z-Shave' attack), because S2-only inclusion is not enforced.
findings.impact: An attacker in RF range at inclusion time can force S0, recover the network key via the hardcoded all-zero temporary key, and take control of the device despite S2 support being present.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce S2-only inclusion with no S0 fallback; reject any KEX_REPORT that requests a lower security class; require out-of-band DSK verification at inclusion.

findings.title: Z-Wave Command Replay Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce S2, whose Singlecast nonce/SPAN sequencing rejects replayed frames; never operate actuators over unencrypted or S0 command classes.
findings.description: A previously captured unencrypted (or S0) Z-Wave command frame was retransmitted and the device acted on it, confirming no effective anti-replay protection.
findings.impact: An attacker can record a legitimate command (lock/unlock, on/off) and replay it later to actuate the device without ever possessing the network key.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce S2, whose Singlecast nonce/SPAN sequencing rejects replayed frames; never operate actuators over unencrypted or S0 command classes.

findings.title: Z-Wave S2 Secure Class Confirmed
findings.remediation_brief: Confirm every node is S2 (no S0-only devices) and that the controller enforces S2-only inclusion with no S0 fallback; verify DSK out-of-band at inclusion.
findings.description: The network was observed using the S2 Security_2 command class (CC 0x9F), which performs an ECDH (Curve25519) authenticated key exchange with an out-of-band DSK and provides per-frame nonce-based anti-replay.
findings.impact: S2 traffic is not passively decryptable or trivially replayable; this is the desired posture, though it must be confirmed for ALL nodes with no S0 fallback permitted.
findings._x_remediation: Confirm every node is S2 (no S0-only devices) and that the controller enforces S2-only inclusion with no S0 fallback; verify DSK out-of-band at inclusion.

findings.title: Z-Wave S0 NonceGet Denial-of-Service Exposure
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate off S0 to S2; rate-limit NonceGet handling; drop NonceGet requests from NodeIDs that are not actively transacting.
findings.description: The Z-Wave gateway accepts unauthenticated S0 NonceGet requests, allowing an attacker to flood NonceGet frames (the 'S0-No-More' attack) and exhaust the gateway's nonce state so legitimate S0 encryption is blocked.
findings.impact: A denial-of-service that halts the whole S0 mesh — including safety-relevant devices such as locks and sensors — requiring only RF range and a valid included NodeID.
findings._x_remediation: Migrate off S0 to S2; rate-limit NonceGet handling; drop NonceGet requests from NodeIDs that are not actively transacting.

findings.title: Z-Wave Testing SKIPPED — No SDR or Sniffer Available
findings.remediation_brief: Attach a HackRF One (EZ-Wave / scapy-radio), a CatSniffer with Sub-GHz firmware, or an RTL-SDR (waving-z / rtl_433), install the Z-Wave capture tooling, and re-run the module to actually assess the interface.
findings.description: Z-Wave testing was not performed because no SDR/sniffer was selected, no capture CLI was installed, or no Z-Wave traffic was observed on the selected frequency. This is an honesty marker so the operator is not misled into thinking the interface was assessed.
findings.impact: The Z-Wave attack surface remains unassessed; any unencrypted control, S0 key-exchange, downgrade, or replay weakness would go undetected until the module is re-run with working capture hardware.
findings._x_remediation: Attach a HackRF One (EZ-Wave / scapy-radio), a CatSniffer with Sub-GHz firmware, or an RTL-SDR (waving-z / rtl_433), install the Z-Wave capture tooling, and re-run the module to actually assess the interface.

findings.title: LoRa Transmission Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile the transmitting radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield LoRa interfaces that are not required and document expected channels/spreading factors.
findings.description: LoRa radio transmissions were captured on the device's regional ISM band (433/868/915 MHz) during passive scanning, including frame count and observed MHDR MType(s).
findings.impact: Confirms a live LoRa wireless attack surface and provides the frames needed to target the subsequent LoRaWAN activation, key, replay, and payload tests.
findings._x_remediation: Reconcile the transmitting radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield LoRa interfaces that are not required and document expected channels/spreading factors.

findings.title: LoRaWAN Network Traffic Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Confirm the LoRaWAN deployment is authorised and inventoried; ensure the network server enforces monotonic frame counters and secure join handling.
findings.description: LoRaWAN protocol traffic (Join and/or MAC data frames identifiable by their MHDR/FHDR structure and DevAddr) was identified in the passive capture.
findings.impact: Confirms a LoRaWAN network is in range and reachable to a passive listener, exposing DevAddr and frame-counter metadata used to assess replay and key-management weaknesses.
findings._x_remediation: Confirm the LoRaWAN deployment is authorised and inventoried; ensure the network server enforces monotonic frame counters and secure join handling.

findings.title: Raw LoRa Payload Transmitted Without Encryption
findings.remediation_brief: Encrypt and authenticate the application payload (AES-CTR/GCM with a per-device key and a monotonic counter/nonce), or adopt LoRaWAN and rely on its MIC and FRMPayload encryption.
findings.description: A proprietary (non-LoRaWAN) LoRa frame carried an application payload that decodes to printable/structured cleartext, indicating the payload is transmitted with no encryption or message integrity check.
findings.impact: Any passive listener in radio range reads sensor/telemetry data directly, and — absent a MIC — can forge or replay commands to the device, undermining confidentiality and integrity of the RF link.
findings._x_remediation: Encrypt and authenticate the application payload (AES-CTR/GCM with a per-device key and a monotonic counter/nonce), or adopt LoRaWAN and rely on its MIC and FRMPayload encryption.

findings.title: LoRaWAN ABP Activation — Static Session Keys
findings.remediation_brief: Prefer OTAA so fresh session keys are derived per join; where ABP is mandatory, persist frame counters across reboots (never reset them) and rotate the ABP session keys on a defined schedule.
findings.description: The device is activated by ABP (Activation By Personalization), so the NwkSKey and AppSKey are provisioned as static, long-lived key material instead of being derived per session by an OTAA join.
findings.impact: On a device reset the frame counter returns to zero while the keys are unchanged, so the AES-CTR keystream/IV is reused across sessions — enabling known-plaintext / crib-dragging recovery of payloads and replay of previously captured uplinks.
findings._x_remediation: Prefer OTAA so fresh session keys are derived per join; where ABP is mandatory, persist frame counters across reboots (never reset them) and rotate the ABP session keys on a defined schedule.

findings.title: LoRaWAN OTAA Join Replay — Missing DevNonce Tracking
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade to LoRaWAN 1.1, which enforces a monotonic DevNonce counter and join-server nonce tracking; where 1.0.x is required, persist the full DevNonce history per device and reject any repeat.
findings.description: The device uses OTAA under LoRaWAN 1.0.x, where the end device cannot detect a repeated Join-Accept and the network server only remembers a bounded number of recent DevNonce values, so a captured Join-Request can be replayed after that window rolls over.
findings.impact: An attacker replays a captured Join-Request to force a re-join and session-key reset, enabling denial-of-service against the node or pinning it to attacker-observable key material derived from replayed nonces.
findings._x_remediation: Upgrade to LoRaWAN 1.1, which enforces a monotonic DevNonce counter and join-server nonce tracking; where 1.0.x is required, persist the full DevNonce history per device and reject any repeat.

findings.title: LoRaWAN Default or Weak AppKey
findings.remediation_brief: Provision a unique, random, secret AppKey per device at manufacture; never print, log, share, or derive it from public identifiers; store it in a secure element and rotate immediately on suspected compromise.
findings.description: The device's LoRaWAN root AppKey (OTAA) or session keys (ABP) are default, all-zero, sequential, vendor-shared, or derivable from the public DevEUI — i.e. a hard-coded or guessable credential.
findings.impact: Recovering the AppKey lets an attacker derive the session keys, decrypt every FRMPayload, forge a valid MIC, and fully impersonate the device — collapsing the entire LoRaWAN security model for that node and any others sharing the key.
findings._x_remediation: Provision a unique, random, secret AppKey per device at manufacture; never print, log, share, or derive it from public identifiers; store it in a secure element and rotate immediately on suspected compromise.

findings.title: LoRaWAN Missing Frame-Counter Validation
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce strict monotonic frame-counter validation at the network server (reject any FCnt <= last seen), enable 32-bit frame counters, and alert on counter resets or rollovers.
findings.description: The network accepted a LoRaWAN uplink whose frame counter (FCnt) was equal to or lower than a previously-seen value — observed as a repeated FCnt in the capture, or confirmed by an authorized replay — indicating frame-counter validation is not strictly enforced.
findings.impact: Without strict monotonic frame-counter checks an attacker replays captured uplinks to re-trigger device actions or mask live telemetry with stale readings, defeating the protocol's core replay protection.
findings._x_remediation: Enforce strict monotonic frame-counter validation at the network server (reject any FCnt <= last seen), enable 32-bit frame counters, and alert on counter resets or rollovers.

findings.title: LoRaWAN Cleartext Application Payload
findings.remediation_brief: Add end-to-end application-layer encryption/authentication (e.g. AES-GCM with a key held only by the device and the application server) so LoRaWAN network operators cannot read or forge sensitive payloads.
findings.description: The captured FRMPayload decodes to printable/structured data and the application relies solely on LoRaWAN's session-key FRMPayload encryption, with no independent end-to-end application-layer encryption.
findings.impact: Any holder of the session keys — the network server, a compromised join server, or an attacker who recovered a weak/default key — reads the plaintext, and for raw or misconfigured payloads a passive listener may read it directly.
findings._x_remediation: Add end-to-end application-layer encryption/authentication (e.g. AES-GCM with a key held only by the device and the application server) so LoRaWAN network operators cannot read or forge sensitive payloads.

findings.title: LoRaWAN 1.0.x — No Join-Request Replay Protection
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate the network server and end devices to LoRaWAN 1.1, which adds monotonic DevNonce handling and join-server nonce tracking; until then, maximise the DevNonce cache and monitor for repeated joins.
findings.description: The network operates LoRaWAN 1.0.x, in which Join-Request messages carry no replay protection prior to the 1.1 monotonic DevNonce counter — a protocol-version exposure applying to every OTAA device on the network.
findings.impact: The version gap leaves all OTAA joins susceptible to nonce reuse and Join-Request replay, providing a standing foothold for denial-of-service and session-reset attacks independent of any single observed replay.
findings._x_remediation: Migrate the network server and end devices to LoRaWAN 1.1, which adds monotonic DevNonce handling and join-server nonce tracking; until then, maximise the DevNonce cache and monitor for repeated joins.

findings.title: LoRa Testing SKIPPED — No SDR or LoRa Radio Available
findings.remediation_brief: Flash a Heltec LoRa32 v3 or LilyGo LoRa32 with single-channel-sniffer firmware via Quiver, or attach an RTL-SDR / HackRF with rtl-433 and universal-radio-hacker installed, then re-run the module.
findings.description: Gearbox attempted LoRa / LoRaWAN assessment but no usable radio was available: either no hardware was selected, the LoRa32 sniffer board exposed no serial port, or neither rtl_433 nor urh_cli was on PATH.
findings.impact: LoRa / LoRaWAN was NOT tested for this interface, so any radio-layer, key-management, or replay weakness remains unverified and unreported until a capture-capable radio is provided.
findings._x_remediation: Flash a Heltec LoRa32 v3 or LilyGo LoRa32 with single-channel-sniffer firmware via Quiver, or attach an RTL-SDR / HackRF with rtl-433 and universal-radio-hacker installed, then re-run the module.

findings.title: BLE LESC Passkey Recovered from Passive Capture
findings.remediation_brief: Use a fresh, random, single-use passkey per pairing that is never printed, hard-coded, or reused; a passkey a single sniffed pairing reveals provides no MITM protection under LESC.
findings.description: The 6-digit LE Secure Connections Passkey Entry passkey was recovered offline from a passively-captured pairing. In LESC Passkey Entry each of the 20 passkey bits is committed with f4 (AES-CMAC over the cleartext ECDH public keys, the revealed per-round nonce, and one passkey bit); once the nonce is revealed the single bit is brute-forced by matching the captured Pairing Confirm, and the recovery is confirmed independently from the initiator and responder halves.
findings.impact: An attacker who passively sniffs ONE pairing recovers the passkey with no active MITM and no physical access to the printed value. If the passkey is static or reused it authenticates every future session and every unit that shares it, collapsing LESC Passkey Entry to Just Works — full man-in-the-middle and session compromise.
findings._x_remediation: Fresh, random, single-use per-pairing passkey; never printed or reused.
_x_references: Bluetooth Core Spec Vol 3 Part H 2.3.5.6.3

findings.title: SSH Password Authentication Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable PasswordAuthentication and ChallengeResponseAuthentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Require public key authentication exclusively. CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG both mandate disabling password-based SSH login.
findings.description: The SSH server accepts password-based authentication methods (password and/or keyboard-interactive) alongside public key authentication. Password authentication is susceptible to brute-force attacks and does not enforce multi-factor authentication.
findings.impact: An attacker can attempt password brute-force attacks against the SSH service. Even with strong passwords, password authentication lacks the cryptographic assurance of key-based authentication and is incompatible with most MFA implementations. Compliance frameworks including CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs mandate public-key-only SSH authentication.

findings.title: SSH Password-Only Authentication (No Public Key)
findings.remediation_brief: Enable public key authentication and disable PasswordAuthentication and ChallengeResponseAuthentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Generate and deploy SSH key pairs for all authorized users.
findings.description: The SSH server accepts only password-based authentication methods (password and/or keyboard-interactive) with no public key authentication available. This is a significant security weakness — the server cannot accept key-based authentication at all, making brute-force the only barrier to unauthorized access.
findings.impact: Without public key authentication, the SSH server relies entirely on password strength for security. An attacker can mount online brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks with no cryptographic barrier. This configuration violates CIS Benchmark and DISA STIG requirements for SSH hardening.
